title: Changing one thing at a time

files.lesson.md: --- order: 12 unit: rules node: [AC9M7A06 n1, AC9M7A06 n2] uses: [AC9M7A01 n2] # substituting into a formula title: Changing one thing at a time summary: "To see what one variable does to a formula, change only that one and hold the rest still, then read the table. The same test works on a box, on distance and on a square." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A scientist testing a plant changes the light, but not the water. How would you test one letter in a formula the same way?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8301 url: http://127.0.0.1:8301/index.html readySelector: "#sl-h" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: formula.yml#explain-pic, caption: "With $l = 2$ and $w = 3$ held still, a taller box (h = 3) has volume $2 \\times 3 \\times 3 = 18$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@formula.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Only h changes" say: "Hold l and w still. Change only h." clip: - caption: { text: "l = 2 and w = 3 stay fixed. h = 1 gives V = 6.", say: "L and w stay fixed. H is one, so V is six." } - wait: 800 - caption: { text: "Make h bigger, and V grows by 6 each time.", say: "Make h bigger, and V grows by six each time." } - click: Make h bigger - click: Make h bigger - expect: { selector: "body", contains: "2 × 3 × 3" } - wait: 1500 connection: event-budget --- A **formula** has several variables, such as $V = l \times w \times h$. To find out what one variable does to the output, **vary it systematically**: change that one, keep every other variable the same, and write the results in a table. ## Predict: doubling h ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to what doubling h does to V shows whether they see volume as a product, where doubling one factor doubles the output." check: type: predict q: "A box has $l = 2$, $w = 3$ and $h = 2$, so $V = 12$. What is $V$ when $h$ is doubled to 4 and the rest stay the same?" options: ["24", "16", "14", "12"] actual: "24. V = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24: doubling one factor doubles the product." ``` Keep l and w the same. ## Run: change only h ```step stage: run insight: "Moving only h and reading V, with l and w held still, shows the pattern for one variable at a time." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#run", height: 520 } check: { type: board, text: "Keep $l = 2$ and $w = 3$. Move $h$ up from 1 to 4 and watch $V$. Was your prediction right?", when: "l = 2 and w = 3 and h = 4", explain: "V = 6, 12, 18, 24: each step of 1 in h adds 6 to V, because l × w = 6." } ``` Move one slider at a time. Here is what the board shows: | $h$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | |---|---|---|---|---| | $V$ (with $l = 2$, $w = 3$) | 6 | 12 | 18 | 24 | ## Investigate: a fair test ```step stage: investigate insight: "A fair test changes one variable (Tom changes two); a table shows the pattern; some variables matter more than others." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "With $l = 2$ and $w = 3$, $V$ is 6, 12, 18 when $h$ is 1, 2, 3. By how much does $V$ go up for each extra 1 in $h$?" answer: "6" feedback: - ["1", "That is how much h goes up. Look at V: 6 to 12."] explain: "V goes up by 6 each time, which is l × w = 2 × 3." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#tom" text: "Tom wants to know what h does to V. Click the line where his test stops being fair." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: vary-two-at-once explain: "Line 3: he changes w as well as h, so he cannot tell which caused the change in V. Change h alone: V = 2 × 3 × 2 = 12." - check: type: question q: "To find the effect of $w$ on $V = lwh$, what should you do?" options: ["Change w only, and keep l and h the same", "Change l, w and h together", "Change l and h only", "Change w and h together"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "You could not tell which letter did what.", "w is the letter you want to test.", "Then h would also change V."] explain: "Isolate one variable at a time: that is a fair test." ``` ### The pattern in the table Look at the V row. ### A fair test? Read Tom's working. What did he change? ### What to change ## Modify: other formulas ```step stage: modify insight: "The same method on distance and on a square: both variables doubling, a square growing faster than its side, and the variable with the biggest effect." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#distance", height: 520 } tasks: - starter: "formula.yml#distance" hint: ["d = s × t, so 150 = s × 3.", "Try speeds of 30, 40, 50."] check: { type: board, text: "Set the time to 3 hours. Choose the speed so the distance is 150 km.", when: "d = 150 and t = 3", explain: "150 ÷ 3 = 50 km/h." } - check: type: question q: "$d = st$. Speed and time both double. What happens to the distance?" options: ["It becomes 4 times as big", "It doubles", "It stays the same", "It becomes 3 times as big"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The product is multiplied by 2 twice, so it is 4 times as big.", "Both factors went up.", "Think of 2 × 2."] explain: "(2s) × (2t) = 4st: the distance is 4 times as big." - starter: "formula.yml#square" check: { type: board, text: "A square has area $A = s \\times s$. Make the side 6 cm. What does the area become?", when: "A = 36", explain: "6 × 6 = 36 cm². Doubling the side from 3 to 6 made the area 4 times as big (9 to 36)." } - check: type: question q: "$V = lwh$ with $l = 2$, $w = 3$, $h = 4$ (V = 24). Adding 1 to just one variable, which gives the biggest V?" options: ["Adding 1 to l (V = 36)", "Adding 1 to w (V = 32)", "Adding 1 to h (V = 30)", "They all give the same V"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Adding 1 to w gives 2 × 4 × 4 = 32.", "Adding 1 to h gives 2 × 3 × 5 = 30.", "Try each: 36, 32 and 30."] explain: "l is the smallest, so one more makes the biggest proportional change: 3 × 3 × 4 = 36." ``` ### Find the speed Hold the time at 3. ### Both double ### Side and area ### The biggest change ## Practise: vary and describe ```step stage: practise insight: "Reading tables, single changes and a substitution review, mixed; forgetting to hold the others is the planted slip; the substitution review keeps formulas fresh." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#box", height: 520 } tasks: - check: type: answer q: "$V = lwh$ with $l = 2$, $w = 3$, $h = 4$. What is $V$?" answer: "24" explain: "2 × 3 × 4 = 24." - check: type: answer q: "Now change only $w$, from 3 to 4. What is $V$?" answer: "32" feedback: - ["28", "l and h stay at 2 and 4: 2 × 4 × 4."] explain: "2 × 4 × 4 = 32." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Which two stay the same, $l$ and $h$? What is $l \\times h$?", answer: 8, explain: "l = 2 and h = 4 stay put: 2 × 4 = 8. Then w is the only one that changes." } - check: type: answer q: "$d = st$ with $s = 60$ km/h. The time doubles from 2 to 4 hours. What is $d$ now, in km?" answer: "240" feedback: - ["120", "That is the distance for 2 hours. For 4 hours, 60 × 4."] explain: "60 × 4 = 240 km, double the 120 km for 2 hours." - check: type: answer q: "Review: $P = 2l + 2w$ with $l = 6$ and $w = 4$. What is $P$?" answer: "20" feedback: - ["50", "2l means 2 × l, not the digits side by side."] explain: "2 × 6 + 2 × 4 = 12 + 8 = 20." ``` ### Find V ### Change w ### Change t ### Review: substitution ## Make: a test of your own ```step stage: make insight: "Choosing numbers to meet a target then describing the effect of each variable puts the method to use." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#box", height: 520 } hint: ["Find three numbers up to 6 that multiply to 60.", "Try l = 6: then w × h must be 10."] check: { type: board, text: "Make a box with volume 60 where $l > w > h$ (all different).", when: "V = 60 and l > w and w > h", explain: "For example l = 5, w = 4, h = 3 (60), or l = 6, w = 5, h = 2 (60)." } ``` Now write a table (on paper or in a spreadsheet) that varies $h$ from 1 to 6 for your box, and describe in a sentence what happens to $V$ as $h$ goes up. ## Make: change the ticket price on paper ```step stage: make insight: "A fair test changes one number and holds the rest still; the paper task makes them choose which numbers stay put." hint: ["Work out the profit as it is first.", "Only the ticket price changes. Keep the costs and the number of people."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A school event has fixed costs of 200 dollars and a cost of 4 dollars per head. Tickets are 10 dollars and 60 people come, so $\\text{profit} = \\text{price} \\times n - (\\text{fixed} + \\text{cost} \\times n)$ (all made up for the task). Change only the ticket price, from 10 to 11 dollars. What is the new profit, in dollars?" steps: - ["Now: $10 \\times 60 - (200 + 4 \\times 60) = 600 - 440 = 160$", "work out the starting profit"] - ["Keep $n = 60$, fixed 200 and cost 4 the same", "a fair test changes one number only"] - ["$11 \\times 60 - 440 = 660 - 440 = 220$", "the costs are still 440"] - ["Profit goes up by $220 - 160 = 60$", "each extra dollar of price brings 60 more, one per person"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Raising the price from 10 to 11. What happens to the costs, 200 + 4 × 60 = 440?" options: - "They stay at 440, because only the price changed" - "They go up by 1" - "They are worked out again with 11 in place of 4" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Nothing in the costs depends on the ticket price.", "The 4 is the cost per head, not the price. It does not change."] answer: "220" feedback: - ["600", "That is the takings at 10 dollars. Use 11, then take away the costs."] - ["161", "Raising the price by 1 dollar brings in 1 dollar from each of the 60 people, not 1 dollar in all."] criteria: - "I wrote down which numbers stay the same before I changed the price." - "I worked out the starting profit and the new profit with the same costs." - "I can say why the profit went up by 60." explain: "Costs stay at 200 + 4 × 60 = 440. Takings are 11 × 60 = 660, so profit is 220: 60 more than the 160 before. In real life a higher price may mean fewer people come." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. Organisers test one number at a time like this in a budget spreadsheet: "what if we raise the price by a dollar?" Work out both profits, then type the new one. **Also used in** - **Event budgets.** A spreadsheet tests one change at a time: the price, the numbers or the costs. - **Science experiments.** A fair test changes one thing and keeps everything else the same. - **Spreadsheets and simulations.** Every "what if" is one input changed while the rest are held still. ```teacher summary: Students vary one variable at a time in V = lwh, d = st and A = s², write the results as a table and describe the effect (AC9M7A06, nodes 1 and 2). time: 35 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 8 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 9 min goals: - I can change one variable and hold the others still. - I can describe in words what happens to the output. - I can say which variable has the biggest effect, and why. struggle: Holding the others still. Ask students to say which letters stay the same before they move a slider. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need to substitute into a formula (Substituting into formulas in Algebra). The one idea: to see what one letter does, change only that letter. Changing two at once makes it impossible to tell which did what (Tom's mistake). The wider idea is that a variable's effect depends on the formula: in V = lwh, doubling any one factor doubles V; in A = s², doubling s makes A four times as big. The second Modify question and the last are about comparing effects. The elaborations suggest spreadsheets. The Make task ends with a table: let students build it in a spreadsheet with a formula in the cells, so changing one cell updates the row. Machine-learning models are formulas with very many variables tuned in the same way (a talking point only). running: - "Predict: ask what is staying the same." - "Run: ask students to say the pattern in V before moving the next slider." - "Investigate: ask Tom what he should change." - "Modify: ask whether the distance question works for any speed." - "Make: ask for the table, then the sentence." - "Paper: the event budget is worked in books; the page marks the new profit (220) and that the costs stay at 440. Books out, then ask which numbers were held still." stuck: - see: A student moves two sliders and describes the result. ask: Which slider caused that change? fix: Change one, write down V, then change the next. - see: A student says doubling the side doubles the area. ask: What is 6 × 6 compared with 3 × 3? fix: "A square's area has the side twice: doubling gives 4 times." - see: A student reads 2l as 2 and l side by side. ask: What does the working on the board show between 2 and l? fix: 2l means 2 × l. stretch: In d = st, find three different pairs of s and t that give d = 120. What pattern do you see? Which graph would show it? support: Give a printed table with l and w filled in and a blank row for V. leads: > This completes AC9M7A06. Where it leads: formulas in a spreadsheet, and changing the subject of a formula (Algebra, Year 8). exit: q: In V = lwh with l = 2, w = 3, h = 4, h goes to 8 and nothing else changes. What is V? a: "48: 2 × 3 × 8, double the 24 it was." explain: > To see what one variable does in a formula, **change that variable only** and keep the others the same, then record the results in a table. In $V = lwh$, doubling any one variable doubles $V$. In $A = s \times s$, doubling $s$ makes $A$ four times as big. ```

# Formula boards for "Changing one thing at a time".

# region: run
widget: formula
formula: V = lwh
slider l: 1, 6, 2
slider w: 1, 6, 3
slider h: 1, 6, 1
units: cm³
# endregion

# region: explain
widget: formula
formula: V = lwh
slider l: 1, 6, 2
slider w: 1, 6, 3
slider h: 1, 6, 1
# endregion

# region: explain-pic
widget: formula
formula: V = lwh
slider l: 1, 6, 2
slider w: 1, 6, 3
slider h: 3, 6, 3
# endregion

# region: distance
widget: formula
formula: d = st
slider s: 10, 100, 50, 10
slider t: 1, 6, 2
units: km
# endregion

# region: square
widget: formula
formula: A = ss
slider s: 1, 10, 3
units: cm²
# endregion

# region: box
widget: formula
formula: V = lwh
slider l: 1, 6, 1
slider w: 1, 6, 1
slider h: 1, 6, 1
units: cm³
# endregion
files.working.txt:
# Tom's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: tom
Tom wants to know what h does to V = lwh.
He sets l = 2, w = 3 and h = 1, so V = 6.
Then he changes h to 2 and w to 4, so V = 16.
V went from 6 to 16, so doubling h made V go up by 10.
# endregion
